intro: We use “be going to” to talk about plans and intentions (“I'm going to change jobs”) and to predict something when we can already see the signs (“Look at those clouds — it's going to rain”).
objectifs: Form “be going to” + base verb with every subject, in all forms.
Talk about a plan or intention decided before speaking.
Make a prediction based on something you can see now.
Understand “gonna” in speech and know when not to write it.

texte: Use the present of “to be” (am / is / are), then “going to” and the base verb. Only “be” changes with the subject; “going to” + base verb never changes.
Negative: add not after be (I'm not going to, she isn't going to). Question: put be before the subject (Are you going to…?). Short answers: Yes, I am. / No, she isn't.
exemples: What are you going to do this weekend?
Is it going to be expensive? — No, it isn't.

texte: Use “be going to” for a decision you made before the moment of speaking: a plan, an intention, a resolution. Nothing needs to be booked or organised, but the decision exists.
Common time words: tomorrow, next week, next year, this summer, soon, one day.
exemples: I'm going to learn Spanish next year.
We're going to paint the kitchen this weekend.
She isn't going to accept the job in Ottawa.

texte: We also use “be going to” to predict something when we can see now what makes it likely: a sign, some evidence, a situation that has already started.
Ask yourself: “Can I see it coming?” If yes, going to is natural.
exemples: Look at those dark clouds. It's going to rain.
Be careful! You're going to fall!
The score is 3–0 with five minutes left. Cameroon are going to win.
Evidence: the score. In British English, a team often takes a plural verb.

texte: With the verb “go”, people often just say “I'm going to the market” (present continuous) instead of “I'm going to go to the market”. Both are correct; the second one is a bit heavy but common in speech.

“Gonna” is the fast pronunciation of “going to” + verb. You hear it everywhere in films and songs, but do not write it in an email or careful text. Note: “gonna” only replaces “going to” before a verb, never “going to” + a place (not “I'm gonna the shop”).

“Will” (lesson 49) is used, among other things, for decisions made at the moment of speaking, and the present continuous (lesson 50) for fixed arrangements. Here, remember: decision already made or visible evidence → going to.

lignes: I'm going to buy a new laptop.
The phone's ringing. — I'll answer it.

formule: am / is / are + going to + base verb
prononciation: In everyday speech, “going to” + verb often becomes /ˈɡʌnə/ (gonna) or /ˈɡəʊɪŋ tə/ with a weak to: I'm going to call /aɪm ˈɡʌnə kɔːl/.
In very fast conversation, “I'm going to” can even sound like /ˈaɪmənə/. Learn to recognise it; you don't have to copy it.
Contractions are normal in speech: I'm, you're, he's, we're, they're; and isn't / aren't in negatives.
In “Are you going to…?”, the voice goes up at the end of a yes / no question and down in a Wh- question (What are you going to do?).
erreurs: She's going to visits her aunt.
She's going to visit her aunt.
After going to: base verb, no -s.
Are you going to working tomorrow?
Are you going to work tomorrow?
We go to move next month.
We're going to move next month.
The structure is be going to, not go to.
Make the question with be, not do.

dialogue.contexte: Two friends, Ama and Lucas, talk about their summer plans in a café in Lille.
lignes: So, what are you going to do this summer?
I'm going to visit my family in Accra. I'm going to stay for a month.
Lucky you! Are you going to work there?
No, I'm not. I'm going to relax. And you?
I'm going to look for a new job. I'm not going to stay at the bank.
An intention and a negative intention.
Good idea. Oh, look at the sky — it's going to rain.
Again? I'm going to buy a bigger umbrella!

mots: What are your plans for the weekend?
something you have decided to do; to decide what to do
I intend to finish my degree.
to want and plan to do something
We're going to move next year.
in a short time from now
I'm going to call her tomorrow.
the space above the earth where you see clouds and the sun
a white or grey shape in the sky made of water
I'm going to save money for a car.
to keep money to use later; to keep a file on a computer
We're going to have a holiday in Spain.
a time when you do not work and often travel (US: vacation)
He's going to look for a flat.

exercices.consigne: Complete with am, is or are.
items: My sister ___ going to study in Canada.
It ___ going to be hot tomorrow.

exercices.consigne: Complete with the right form of be going to and the verb in brackets.
items: He ___ (not / take) the exam this year.

exercices.titre: 3. Prediction: what is going to happen?
exercices.consigne: Write a prediction with going to from the evidence.
items: He's running very fast to the bus stop and the bus is leaving. (miss the bus)
He's going to miss the bus.
She's very tired and her eyes are closing. (fall asleep)
The glass is at the edge of the table. (fall)

exercices.consigne: Each sentence has one mistake. Write it correctly.
items: Do you going to help me?
Are you going to help me?
She going to start a new job.
She's going to start a new job.
They're going to buys a house.
They're going to buy a house.

exercices.consigne: Write the sentence with going to, then say if it is a plan or a prediction.
items: I'm going to call my mother tonight. (plan)
Be careful, you're going to fall! (prediction)
They aren't going to come tomorrow. (plan / intention)

exercices.consigne: Write five sentences about your plans for next year (at least one negative and one question).
items: Next year I'm going to take an English exam. I'm going to read one book in English every month. I'm not going to watch films with French subtitles anymore. My brother and I are going to visit our cousins in Montreal. What are you going to do?

a_retenir: am / is / are + going to + base verb (never -s or -ing after going to).
Plan or intention decided before speaking: I'm going to change jobs.
Prediction with visible evidence: Look! It's going to rain.
Negative: I'm not / isn't / aren't going to; question: Are you going to…?
Gonna = fast pronunciation of going to + verb: understand it, don't write it.
